extracted.intended_audience: artists, painters, art-critics, and connoisseurs (those evaluating or producing landscape/figure painting)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for assessing and producing truthful tone, aerial perspective, light, and color in painting (especially landscape). Emphasises how materials, viewing distance, and choices between richness and completeness affect truthfulness in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (first sense): quality imparted by illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: “That precious quality of each color laid on, which makes the eye feel both what is the actual color of the object represented, and that it is raised to its apparent pitch by illumination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone is not merely a bright local hue but the sensation caused by illumination raising local color to an apparent pitch. The want of tone is caused when objects look bright in their own positive hue, and not by illumination. Aim to render colors so the eye perceives both their local identity and their modulation by light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone versus aerial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerial perspective is the expression of space by sharpness of edge, vividness of color, etc., assisted by greater pitch of shadow; tone (first sense) requires that there should be the same sum of difference, as well as the same division of differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate tone with aerial perspective: aerial perspective needs only proportionate intensity differences by distance; true tone requires preserving both total range and the relative divisions of differences. Evaluate whether a painting preserves proportional gradations as well as absolute relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of middle tints to light (old masters' method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Old masters make the dark objects in middle distance have precisely the same relation to the light of the sky which they have in nature, but the light being infinitely lowered and shadows deepened in the same degree—'notes of nature played two or three octaves below her key.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method attains a powerful apparent tone at the cost of compressing tonal range: it often produces flat masses with omitted intermediate distances. Recognize this approach as imitative and deliberately selective; it gives strong broad effect but sacrifices many fine gradations of space and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of sacrificing internal relations for apparent tone
rubrics_metrics.description: By lavishing means to obtain one truth (e.g., relation of tree to sky) old masters often omit the greater part of the scene's other truths, making the retained truth false by the absence of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of paintings that secure one striking relation while destroying the relations among parts; truth of the whole requires ordered representation of parts, not only a few conspicuous contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turner's principle: proportional compression of shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner takes pure white for his highest light and lampblack for his deepest shade; between these he makes every degree of shade indicative of separate degree of distance, so that differences bear the same proportion to his sum of possible shade as in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When materials cannot match nature's full extremes, scale the available tonal range proportionally so each step represents a degree of distance—this allows expressing many more intermediate distances (where old masters might express only a few). Examples: Mercury and Argus; contrasts with Poussin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer scientific/truthful systems over deceptive imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The deceptive imitation of nature is inconsistent with real truth,’ and the system which preserves aerial perspective and proportional relations is the only scientific or essentially truthful system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value methods that render true relations of depth, form, and distance even if they lose some seductive imitative effects. Judge pictures by whether they convey factual relations, not only by how convincingly they mimic isolated appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two qualities of light: neutral (white) and colored
rubrics_metrics.description: Light, with reference to the tone it induces on objects, is either to be considered as neutral and white, bringing out local colors with fidelity; or colored, and consequently modifying these local tints with its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which quality of light you represent. Neutral white allows primaries to appear in purity; colored lights (e.g., yellow sunset, rose twilight) will impose hues on local colors and make some colors impossible or necessary. Represent the modifying effect consistently across the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of local color requires white highest light
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If the picture is to be complete in its system of color...it must have white for its highest light, otherwise the purity of one of [the primaries] at least will be impossible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to show full range and purity of local primaries, reserve a neutral (white) highest light. If you choose a colored highest light you accept that some primaries cannot exist in purity and must be modified appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impossible/exaggerated colors for mere richness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some celebrated pictures achieve 'richness and solemnity of color' by exaggerated and impossible means (Titian's distant blue that is too dark and too blue to be aerial), which are beautiful but not truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain color effects—though powerful—are physiologically or atmospherically impossible. Use such exaggeration consciously and accept the trade-off: it may heighten feeling but sacrifices literal truth of atmosphere and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express aerial perspective by intervening mist and proportionate intensity loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerial perspective requires that objects be detached from each other by degrees of intensity in proportion to their distance, often assisted by intervening mist and light (e.g., Turner shows distinct aerial perspective even within a short distance between leaves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render graduated diminution of intensity and increased atmosphere between near and far parts—even among parts of the same tree—to give true recession. Test whether small internal separations (nearest bough to next bough) are indicated, not only object-to-object distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for material limits: paint cannot equal nature's extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's highest light (the sun) and deepest shades (vacuity) far exceed what paint can show; our materials force us to 'run the gauntlet' with white paper as highest light and visibly illumined surface for deepest shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge pigment and medium limitations and adapt: compress tonal range proportionally, choose which truths to prioritize (many intermediate distances vs one strong contrast), and avoid expecting paint to reproduce nature's absolute luminous force or void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer completeness (space/form) over mere richness of tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner sacrifices some richness of tone to gain many 'essential truths'—extension of space, fulness of form, and multiplicity of gradations—because these are more important as matters of truth or fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trade-offs arise, favor representing form and depth with many gradations rather than maximizing seductive single-tone richness. Evaluate works by how well they convey structure and distance, not solely by sumptuous color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone should be consistent and effective at any viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner's pictures retain influence and glow 'at whatever distance we stand,' whereas many pictures (e.g., some Claudes) must be seen close to show their effect and lose light as we retire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tonal organization by viewing at multiple distances; a successful painting's color and tonal effect should read correctly both up close and at a distance. Avoid local passages that look right close but fail when the whole is seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid solecisms: local colors must respond to general light
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures occur when parts (e.g., a vermilion dress in Cuyp) are 'totally unaffected and unwarmed by the golden hue of the rest of the picture' or have little distinction between illumined and shaded parts, making them appear out of sunshine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each local color is modified consistently by the overall light (warmth/coolness) and shows appropriate division between illuminated and shaded parts. Such solecisms make a work fail at a distance and injure its whole effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite multiple tones when climate/altitude demands it
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature often changes tone with elevation and climate; Turner 'unites two, three, or even more separate tones in the same composition' to reflect such variations—cold with warm light, different tones in upper/lower clouds, horizon, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not enforce artificial unity of a single tone across a scene when nature legitimately presents multiple associated tones. Study how different atmospheric bands and elevations carry different tonalities and reconcile them thoughtfully in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render many gradations between highest light and deepest shadow
rubrics_metrics.description: Because nature provides a vast number of subtle steps of gradation, the painter must avoid giving any one inter-distance step the full quantity of difference nature gives (else many other distances are lost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the tonal scale so many small intermediate values are present; distribute the available tonal 'sum' so each division proportionally represents a degree of distance or form. This preserves subtle spatial information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating deepest shadow as merely 'black surface'
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's deepest shades are 'void spaces' from which no light is reflected; paint's deepest tones are reflective black surfaces—if painted like nature's voids they conflict with adjacent painted surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt literal equivalence to nature's voids; instead, treat deepest shadows in a way consistent with paint's reflective properties, and adapt surrounding tones to maintain believable relations of distance and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of color requires careful observation and variation, not uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (Gaspar Poussin's La Riccia) show failures where foliage and masses are painted in uniform dull tints without the delicate color variation of actual scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and render the variety of local colors (subtle shifts in leafage, rocks, road surfaces, distant hues). Uniform application of a single dull color across a mass is a sign of untruth; introduce slight modulations to suggest real color complexity.
